system-design-big-picture-request-flow.s.title: The big picture: what happens when you tap a button
system-design-big-picture-request-flow.s.caption: Follow the numbers. A tap travels to the front door, then to the app, then to the data. Slow jobs wait in a line, and everything keeps notes so people can fix problems.
steps: Your phone or laptop sends a request, like handing a note to a waiter.
A gatekeeper checks the request is safe and sends it the right way.
The app thinks about what you asked and decides what to do.
Notes, photos, and facts you want are kept safe here.
Slow jobs, like making a big report, wait here instead of making you wait.
Helpers pick jobs from the line one by one and finish them.
Logs, counts, and traces record what happened so problems can be found.
You see the result on your screen, ideally in less than a second.

system-design-requirements-to-architectu.title: From what people need to what we build
system-design-requirements-to-architectu.caption: Good design starts with people, not machines. First ask what they need, then count how much, then pick the simplest parts that can do the job.
steps: Write the jobs in plain words: 'save a note', 'find a note'.
Fast? Always on? Safe? These are quality goals.
Guess users, requests, and data size. Write numbers down.
Which part will run out first: speed, space, or money?
Choose the smallest set of boxes that fits the numbers.
Say what you gain and what you give up with each choice.

system-design-browser-to-api-request.svg.title: A web request, step by step
system-design-browser-to-api-request.svg.caption: Before any real work starts, your browser finds the address, makes a safe connection, and gets directed to a healthy server. Only then does the app look at your data.
steps: You type 'notes.example.com'. Computers need a number, not a name.
DNS looks up the name and finds the number address.
TLS locks the road so nobody can read the message on the way.
The front door checks the request and chooses where it goes.
Picks the least busy copy of the app so nobody waits in a long line.
The app checks the rules and builds the answer.
It first checks the fast shelf (cache) and then the big storeroom (database).
The answer goes back the same road to your screen.

system-design-api-layered-architecture.s.title: Layers: a school with different jobs in different rooms
system-design-api-layered-architecture.s.caption: Each layer has one job and only talks to the layer next to it. That way you can change the storage without touching the screens, and the other way around.
steps: What people see and tap. It does not know how data is stored.
Takes requests, checks the shape, and sends back answers.
Decides the steps: 'first check, then save, then tell'.
The real rules of the business, like 'a title can't be empty'.
Knows how to read and write the data, and nothing else.
Database, files, and email: the outside things we plug in.

system-design-database-choice-map.svg.title: Which kind of storage should I pick?
system-design-database-choice-map.svg.caption: Ask what the data looks like and how you will look for it. If you are unsure, start with a normal relational database. It handles most things well.
steps: Is it tidy rows, a bag of notes, small facts, files, or text to search?
Use a relational database (like PostgreSQL). Great for most apps.
Use a key-value store: give a key, get a value, very quickly.
Use a document database when each item has a different shape.
Use a search engine when people type words to find things.
Photos and videos go into object storage, with a pointer in the database.
Do you need 'all or nothing' saves? That points to relational.
Add another storage only when a real need appears.

system-design-cache-aside-flow.svg.title: A cache is a sticky note on your desk
system-design-cache-aside-flow.svg.caption: Look at the sticky note first (cache). If the answer is there, great. If not, go to the big storeroom, copy the answer onto a sticky note, and keep going. When facts change, throw the old note away.
steps: A visitor wants a note. We check the sticky notes first.
The answer is on the sticky note. We reply instantly.
No sticky note yet, so we must go and look in the storeroom.
The database finds the real answer. It is slower, but always right.
We copy the answer into the cache so the next person is faster.
Someone edits the note. The old sticky note is now wrong.
We remove the old cache entry so nobody sees outdated words.

system-design-async-job-queue-flow.svg.title: A ticket counter for slow jobs
system-design-async-job-queue-flow.svg.caption: A slow job gets a ticket and goes into a line. A helper does the work in the background while the visitor goes on with their day. If a job keeps failing, it goes to a special 'problem box' for a person to look at.
steps: Someone asks for a huge PDF report. That takes minutes.
The app answers quickly: 'Got it. Your ticket number is 42.'
The job waits in a queue. The line has a size limit.
A worker takes the next job when it is free.
The ticket number lets you ask: 'Is it done yet?'
The finished file is saved and the status says 'done'.
If it fails, the helper waits a bit and tries again a few times.
After too many failures the job goes to a dead-letter box for a human.

system-design-reliable-request-flow.svg.title: When something breaks, don't make it worse
system-design-reliable-request-flow.svg.caption: Wait only a little (timeout), try again carefully (retry with waiting), and stop calling a broken helper for a while (circuit breaker). Always tell the user the truth.
steps: Our app asks another service for something.
Only wait a short time. Waiting forever blocks everyone.
The timer rings. The helper is slow or broken.
Wait a bit, then wait longer next time, with a little randomness.
The circuit breaker 'trips' and stops sending more calls.
Show a saved copy or a clear message instead of a crash.
After a pause, send one test call to see if it works again.
The helper answers, and the breaker closes.

system-design-sharding-and-replication.s.title: Copies and slices of data
system-design-sharding-and-replication.s.caption: Replication makes copies so many people can read and so we survive a crash. Sharding cuts the data into slices so no single machine holds everything. Copies can be a moment behind.
steps: All writes go to the primary, the 'master copy'.
Replicas copy the primary. Many readers can use them at once.
A new write takes a moment to arrive. A reader might see old data.
One machine cannot hold everything or answer fast enough.
Shard A holds names A to M, shard B holds N to Z.
A rule (the shard key) sends each request to the right slice.
One very popular key makes one shard busy: a hot key.
If the primary dies, a replica is promoted to take its place.

system-design-security-boundaries.svg.title: Doors and guards: where we check
system-design-security-boundaries.svg.caption: Every door has a guard. The browser is not trusted. The server checks who you are and what you may touch, every time, and only the guards hold the keys.
steps: Anyone can open developer tools. Never trust what the browser says.
Checks the secure connection and blocks too many requests.
Authentication: check the login, token, or session.
Authorization: is this note yours? Is this action allowed?
It uses its own minimum key, not a master key.
Only the app can reach them. No direct path from the internet.
Passwords and keys live in protected settings, not in code.
Write down what happened, but never write passwords or private text.

system-design-observability-three-pillar.title: Three ways to see what your system is doing
system-design-observability-three-pillar.caption: Logs are a diary, metrics are a scoreboard, and traces are a trip itinerary. A request ID ties them together so you can follow one story from start to end.
steps: We give it a unique request ID, like a name tag.
Short notes of what happened, each with the request ID.
Counts and timings: how many requests, how fast, how many errors.
Shows which services the request visited and how long each took.
The error count jumps, or answers become slow.
The right person is told, with a note about what to check first.
Search the logs and trace to find exactly where it broke.
Fix it, then write down what we learned so it does not happen again.

system-design-deployment-and-disaster-re.title: Shipping safely and recovering when things go wrong
system-design-deployment-and-disaster-re.caption: Build one package, test it, and roll it out in small steps. Keep backups and practice restoring them, because a backup you never tried is only a hope.
steps: Turn the code into one tested, numbered package.
Send it to a few servers first, then more.
Smoke tests ask: does it start? Can it reach the database?
Errors go up after the release.
Go back to the last version that worked.
Copy the data to a safe place regularly.
Try bringing the data back. Time how long it takes.
Switch to the second location and keep serving people.

system-design-tm-schedule-e2e.svg.title: One schedule app, from tap to saved data
system-design-tm-schedule-e2e.svg.caption: A worked example: a manager changes a shift. We follow the request from the screen to the database and see where things can fail and how we handle each failure.
steps: The screen sends the new shift time to the app.
The app checks this is a signed-in manager of this store.
Is the date real? Is the end after the start?
The schedule row and its history note are saved together.
A message goes in a queue so notifications are sent later.
The manager sees a success message right away.
The app says 'try again soon'. It never says 'saved' when it was not.
Logs and counters show how many saves worked and how fast.

system-design-architecture-decision-tree.title: Choosing the smallest design that works
system-design-architecture-decision-tree.caption: Ask simple questions in order. Most apps only need the first box: one well-organized app and one database. Add more pieces only when a question says 'yes, we really need it'.
steps: One app, one database, clear folders. This fits most projects.
Add a cache or a read copy of the database.
Add a queue and workers so people do not wait.
Run several copies of the app behind a load balancer.
Split the data into shards, but only if it is really needed.
Only now think about splitting into services.
Add copies in more than one place and practice failing over.
Every extra box is more to build, pay for, and fix.

java-source-compiler-jvm-flow.svg.title: How a Java program comes to life
java-source-compiler-jvm-flow.svg.caption: You write words humans can read. The compiler translates them into bytecode. The JVM, a helper on every computer, runs the bytecode. That is why the same Java program works on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
steps: A file like Hello.java, in words humans can read.
javac checks for mistakes and translates the file.
A file like Hello.class, written in a language the JVM understands.
A list of folders where Java looks for the pieces it needs.
The Java Virtual Machine turns bytecode into real actions.
You see the output on the screen.
Small programs that confirm your code still does what you meant.

java-types-and-control-flow.svg.title: Values, decisions, and repeating
java-types-and-control-flow.svg.caption: A variable is a labeled box that holds one kind of value. Conditions choose a path, loops repeat work, and methods bundle steps and give back an answer.
steps: A value goes in a box
int age = 10; the box is labeled 'age' and holds whole numbers.
Yes runs one block of code. No runs another.
for and while run the same steps again and again.
Give a group of steps a name so you can reuse it.
return hands the result to whoever called the method.

java-class-object-encapsulation.svg.title: Blueprint, house, and locked doors
java-class-object-encapsulation.svg.caption: A class is the blueprint. Every object you make with new is one real house. Private fields are locked rooms. Public methods are the doors you may use, so rules like 'never blank' always hold.
steps: class Note describes what every note has and can do.
new Note("Math") builds one real note from the blueprint.
private String title; stays inside. Others cannot touch it directly.
rename("Science") is the door that everyone may use.
It refuses a blank title before changing anything.
That rule is the invariant. Every Note is always valid.

java-inheritance-composition-polymorphis.title: Is-a and has-a
java-inheritance-composition-polymorphis.caption: Inheritance says 'a Dog is an Animal'. Composition says 'a Car has an Engine'. Polymorphism means you can say 'make a sound' to any animal and each one answers in its own way. Prefer has-a when you can.
steps: Animal has things all animals share, like name.
Dog extends Animal, so it gets those things for free.
Dog gives its own version of speak(): 'Woof'.
Call speak() on any Animal and the real type answers.
A Car holds an Engine and asks it to start.
You can swap the engine without rebuilding the car.

java-interface-and-implementation.svg.title: A promise and different ways to keep it
java-interface-and-implementation.svg.caption: An interface lists what must be possible. The service only knows the promise. Memory and database versions both keep it, so we can swap them for tests or for real life.
steps: NoteService needs to save and find notes.
NoteRepository: save(note) and findById(id). No details.
Keeps notes in a list. Perfect for quick tests.
Saves notes in a real database for real users.
A setting decides which version to plug in.
Both versions must keep the same promise.

java-records-collections-generics.svg.title: Little data cards and the shelves that hold them
java-records-collections-generics.svg.caption: A record is a small, unchangeable data card. A List keeps cards in order, a Set keeps only one of each, and a Map finds a card by its label. Generics tell Java what is on the shelf, like List<Note>.
steps: record Note(int id, String title) holds data, simply.
List<Note>: cards in order. The same card can appear twice.
Set<Note>: no duplicates allowed. Great for 'unique tags'.
Map<Integer, Note>: look up a card by its id quickly.
The <Note> part promises only Notes go in, so no surprises come out.
Order? List. Unique? Set. Lookup by key? Map.

java-exception-and-resource-flow.svg.title: When something goes wrong in Java
java-exception-and-resource-flow.svg.caption: Code in a try block can throw an exception. A catch block handles it. try-with-resources always closes files and connections, even after a failure. The caller gets a short, safe message.
steps: try (var file = open(...)) borrows a file or connection.
Normal steps run. If all goes well, we are finished.
An exception is thrown, like a ball thrown out of the game.
A catch block receives it and decides what to do.
try-with-resources closes the file whether it worked or not.
Return a short, clear error. Keep private details in the log.

java-files-http-jdbc-boundaries.svg.title: Java talking to the outside world
java-files-http-jdbc-boundaries.svg.caption: Files, web calls, and databases are all outside your program. Each one gets a careful wrapper that checks input, sets time limits, and cleans up.
steps: Files.readString(path) with a path kept inside a safe folder.
A JSON library maps text into your records.
HttpClient sends a request, with a timeout.
A class that hides the database details from the rest of the app.
Java's standard way of talking to databases, using ? parameters.
Stores the data safely. Each answer comes back as rows.

java-thread-executor-and-memory.svg.title: Many things at once, and where data lives
java-thread-executor-and-memory.svg.caption: Threads let Java do several things at once. An executor is a team of workers with a size limit. The stack holds the current steps, and the heap holds the objects. Never let work or memory grow without a limit.
steps: Someone asks the server to do something.
A fixed number of worker threads take turns.
One worker runs your task. The others handle more tasks.
If too many tasks arrive, extra ones wait or are refused.
Stack = the steps now. Heap = the objects that live longer.
A task can be asked to stop, and must clean up.

java-testing-and-spring-bridge.svg.title: Testing, and how Spring helps
java-testing-and-spring-bridge.svg.caption: Unit tests check one small piece. HTTP tests check the whole path. Spring creates your objects (beans) and connects them, so the controller, service, and repository snap together.
steps: Checks one method alone, with made-up data.
Sends a real-looking request and checks the response.
Spring reads your classes and sets up beans.
Receives the web request and passes it on.
Talks to the database and returns the result.

python-runtime-and-venv.svg.title: Where your Python code runs
python-runtime-and-venv.svg.caption: Python reads your file line by line. A virtual environment (venv) is a private toolbox for one project, so projects never fight over different versions of the same tool.
steps: A file like app.py with plain, readable lines.
python reads the file and does what each line says.
python -m venv .venv makes a private toolbox for this project.
pip install fastapi puts new tools only in that toolbox.
It becomes a running process on your computer.
Printed text and errors show up on the screen.

python-request-to-response.svg.title: From a click to an answer in FastAPI
python-request-to-response.svg.caption: A browser sends a request over HTTP. An ASGI server hands it to FastAPI, which picks the right route. The route calls the service, the service uses the repository, and the answer returns as JSON.
steps: A browser or app sends GET /notes/1.
The request travels as method, path, headers, and body.
uvicorn receives it and gives it to FastAPI.
Applies the rules: does this note exist?
Reads the data from the database.
FastAPI turns the Python object into JSON.
Status 200 and the note's data appear on screen.

python-fastapi-route-validation.svg.title: FastAPI checks the input before your code runs
python-fastapi-route-validation.svg.caption: FastAPI reads the type hints on your function and checks the incoming data. If it does not match, FastAPI answers with a helpful error and your function is never called.
steps: It carries parts: path, query, and a JSON body.
def create(note: NoteIn) tells FastAPI what to expect.
Pydantic checks each field: type, length, required.
FastAPI returns 422 with a clear explanation. Your code is skipped.
Your function receives a clean, typed NoteIn object.
You focus on the real work, not on parsing.
The answer is filtered to only the fields you promised.

python-pydantic-schema-flow.svg.title: Pydantic: a checkpoint for data
python-pydantic-schema-flow.svg.caption: Pydantic compares incoming JSON with a model you wrote. Good data becomes a clean Python object. Bad data becomes a clear list of what is wrong.
steps: class NoteIn(BaseModel) lists the fields and rules.
Pydantic checks and converts values, like '12' to 12.
note.title and note.pages are ready to use safely.
A response model chooses which fields to send back.
Missing or wrong fields give a 422 with details.

python-layered-api.svg.title: Layers in a FastAPI app
python-layered-api.svg.caption: Each layer has one job. The route talks HTTP, the service holds the rules, and the repository talks to the database. Dependencies are handed in, so each layer can be tested alone.
steps: Reads the request and returns the response. Nothing more.
Depends() hands the route what it needs, like a service or login.
Business rules: trim the title, reject blanks, check duplicates.
SQL lives here. The service never sees SQL.
SQLite for learning, PostgreSQL for real use.
Swap in a fake repository to test the service alone.

python-sqlite-postgresql-boundary.svg.title: One promise, two databases
python-sqlite-postgresql-boundary.svg.caption: The repository is a promise: save, find, delete. SQLite keeps it in one file for learning. PostgreSQL is the big shared database for real apps. The rest of the code cannot tell the difference.
steps: A short list of actions the service may use.
Stores data in one local file. Easy to start.
A shared server database for many users at once.
An environment setting picks which version runs.
Numbered scripts change tables safely over time.

python-authentication-security-boundary..title: Who are you, and what may you do?
python-authentication-security-boundary..caption: The client sends a token. The API checks the token to learn who you are (authentication), then checks whether this note is yours (authorization). If not, the answer is 403 or 404.
steps: Send a username and password over a secure connection.
The server answers with a signed token, like a wristband.
The client attaches the token to every request.
Is it real, unexpired, and signed by us? That is authentication.
Does this note belong to this person? That is authorization.
Return 403 or 404 and never leak private details.

python-async-worker-job-flow.svg.title: Slow work in the background
python-async-worker-job-flow.svg.caption: The API answers right away with a job ID. A worker does the slow work and updates the status. The client can poll with the ID or cancel the job.
steps: Export all notes to a PDF: it may take minutes.
The job waits in a bounded line.
It makes progress and saves its status.
It tries again a few times with growing waits.
GET /jobs/42 says queued, running, done, or failed.
The worker stops and cleans up its files.
The status becomes done with a link to the file.

python-testing-openapi-loop.svg.title: Test, read the docs, fix, repeat
python-testing-openapi-loop.svg.caption: FastAPI makes a live API guide called OpenAPI. Tests call your API like a client and check both success and failure. A failing test shows what to fix.
steps: Use pytest and TestClient to call the route.
pytest tells you what passed and what failed.
Read the message. It points to the exact problem.
Change the route or the rule, then run again.
OpenAPI shows every route and lets you try it.
Make sure the docs and the real answers still match.

python-deployment-health.svg.title: Packing and shipping a FastAPI app
python-deployment-health.svg.caption: Pin your tools in a lock file, build a container that has everything, send settings in from outside, and check health after starting. If it fails, roll back.
steps: A lock file records the exact libraries you tested.
Docker packs your app and its tools into one box.
Passwords and addresses come from the environment, not the code.
The app starts and listens on a port.
/health says alive. /ready says the database is reachable.
Make one real request to be sure it works.
Start the previous container and look at the logs.
